observations.text: The process starts when a customer sends us a request for a quotation. Once we get that request, we record it, check the customer’s information in our CRM, and then create the quotation in our quoting system using the customer and pricing information. The intended outcome is to produce an accurate quotation that we can send to the customer by email.

Sure. In our team, the sales staff handle those steps. Typically, whoever receives the quotation request—usually one of us in sales—records it, checks the customer’s info in the CRM, and then creates the quotation in the quoting system. It’s pretty much the same person doing all three steps for a given request.

We check things like the customer’s contact details, maybe their account status, and any relevant pricing information we have on file. If the customer info isn’t found or is incomplete, we’d usually follow up with the customer or check with whoever handles that account to get the missing details before we proceed with creating the quotation. There’s no special branch or condition beyond that—we just make sure we have what we need to make the quotation accurate.

The pricing information comes from our quoting system—it’s already set up in there, based on our standard price lists and any customer-specific agreements we have on file. When I create the quotation, I pull the pricing from the system for that customer and the products or services they’re asking about. I don’t determine the prices myself; I just use what’s in the system.

That’s a fair question. Recording the request first is just a way to keep track of what came in and when—so we have a record of the request itself. It also helps us make sure we don’t lose track of anything, especially if there are multiple requests coming in. After that, we check the customer info and then create the quotation. It’s basically a logical order to make sure we have everything we need before we put the quotation together.

Checking the customer’s information in the CRM is necessary because we need to make sure we’re working with the correct and up-to-date details for that customer—like their contact info and account status. That way, the quotation we create is accurate and goes to the right person, and we’re not using outdated or incorrect information. It’s a basic verification step before we move on to creating the quotation.

Creating the quotation in the quoting system is necessary because that’s where the pricing and product information is pulled from, and it’s the tool we use to actually generate the quotation document. It ensures the quotation is consistent and accurate based on the data we have in the system. Without that step, we wouldn’t have a proper quotation to send to the customer.

Sending the quotation by email is necessary because that’s how we deliver the quotation to the customer—it’s the standard way we communicate it to them. After sending, there’s nothing else that happens on our side for that particular quotation, unless the customer comes back with questions or changes. That’s basically the end of the process for us.

If the customer information is missing or incomplete, following up is necessary because we can’t create an accurate quotation without the correct details. We need to get the missing information from the customer or from whoever handles that account before we can proceed. It’s just a practical step to make sure we have what we need to do the job properly.

I think the main flow is what I’ve described—receiving the request, checking the customer info, creating the quotation, and sending it by email. I can’t think of any other variations or special cases beyond that.

The receive_request step is necessary because that’s what starts the whole process. Without the customer sending us a request, there’s nothing for us to work on—no quotation to prepare or send. It’s the trigger that sets everything else in motion.
